{"title":"Pubky Updates: April 18, 2025","body":"

Hey Pubky crew!


We've just pushed a fresh batch of updates focused on polishing the frontend, squashing bugs, and making your experience smoother.


Here's what’s new 👇


✨ New Features


  1. - Header Notification Counter — You’ll now see a visual counter in the header to keep track of activity at a glance.
  2. - Unlimited Custom Feeds — Go wild. You can now create as many custom feeds as your heart desires.
  3. - New Profile Tags UI — Profiles now look sharper with a cleaner, more intuitive tags layout.
  4. - Minor UI Touch-ups — Smoother edges and better vibes throughout the app.



🐞 Bug Fixes

Huge thanks to the community for helping us spot and squash these:


  1. Sign-in recovery phrase now accepts lowercase input
  2. - Thanks @CARLA for catching this!

  4. Fixed links that were unintentionally adding tags from within post content
  5. - Shoutout to @Reza for reporting this one.

  7. Timestamps no longer say your post is 55 years old 😅
  8. - Thank you @Wijersrob and @bordalix for the heads-up.

  10. Corrected singular/plural in “time ago” displays
  11. - Nice catch @bordalix!

  13. Other minor bugs: Cleaned up with help from the awesome Synonym team behind the scenes.


Thanks again to everyone for testing, reporting, and building alongside us — you’re helping shape Pubky into something really special!


"}

{"title":"Bitcoin Does Not Scale: A Real Solution","body":"

Bitcoin doesn’t scale ... and that’s the point, right? Bitcoin scales assurance, not transactions. When people ignore this, they reach for soft-fork wishlists, exotic rollups, and new blockchains. All of that adds complexity which quietly re-introduces trust, concentrated in fewer and fewer hands. Meanwhile, the world already “scales Bitcoin” every day by flowing into custodians, wrapped-BTC, and popular alt-chains. People accepted new trust assumptions.


This essay lays out a cleaner mental model for thinking about Bitcoin scaling topics, and a new solution.

  1. How Bitcoin doesn’t (and shouldn’t) scale throughput.
  2. How “make L1 faster” and “just add a new L2” miss the point.
  3. How the market has already scaled via alt rails, by concentrating trust.
  4. The missing piece: a purely peer-to-peer trust fabric that treats trust as a first-class design variable.
  5. The recommendation: mutual credit with bounded risk, periodic Bitcoin settlement, and a credible exit. Tabs, not chains.


The uncomfortable truth: Bitcoin doesn’t scale transactions

If everyone keeps the ability to verify their money without permission, every verifier must verify. The cost to validate rises with total activity. To keep the marginal verifier cheap, you must keep global activity on L1 scarce. That’s not a bug; it’s how we preserve decentralization.


Constraints you can’t wish away:

  1. Propagation & physics: Bigger/faster blocks increase orphan risk and centralize miners.
  2. State bloat: More throughput -> larger UTXO set -> fewer sovereign full nodes.
  3. Security budget: Long-term safety depends on fees; making blockspace abundant kills fees, and with them, deterrence.
  4. DoS & policy: Relaxing relay/standardness rules for speed opens cheap attack surfaces.
  5. Ossification: The system resists sweeping complexity because global coordination is expensive, by design.


A permissionless, globally replicated ledger cannot scale TPS without centralizing verification or introducing trust elsewhere.


Where the current conversation goes wrong

  1. “Just soft-fork X”: Piling on features (covenants, rollups, account models) is not free. More complex consensus = heavier validation = fewer verifiers.
  2. “It’s an L2!”: Most “L2s” trade trust: they depend on operators, committees, sequencers, DA providers, or emergency exits that bottleneck back onto L1 when it matters most.
  3. “We’ll shard/verkle/zk it”: You can compress and batch. You cannot abolish the laws of propagation, validation cost, and economic security.


The net effect: complexity that quietly imports trust, then pretends it didn’t.


How the market already scaled (and why)

Look around. The spillover isn’t picking “pure tech”; it’s picking distribution + trust concentration:

  1. Wrapped BTC on EVMs, BNB, etc.: one (or a few) custodians + deep integrations.
  2. Federated sidechains: n-of-m signers you can name.
  3. Exchange rails: swap to fast coins, move, swap back: pure custodian trust.
  4. High-TPS (cheap) chains: throughput by trusting committees/sequencers.
  5. Lightning hybrids: Spark and Liquid-swaps


These are mostly explicit trust models and hybrids. They \"scale\" because trust scales organizationally and operationally while L1 settlement stays scarce.


The hidden variable is TRUST. Make it explicit!

The right question to ask, when trusting, is:

Trust whom, with what, for how long?


Bitcoin’s comparative advantage is not raw TPS, it’s credible exit and cheap self-verification. That’s the north star. Everything that “scales” should treat Bitcoin as the last-resort judge, not the daily conveyor belt.


We don’t fix scaling by pretending trust disappears. We fix it by engineering trust into the system: making it bounded, local, accountable, and cheap to unwind.


The missing piece: a P2P trust fabric

Instead of more chains or bigger blocks, build a fabric where:

  1. People extend small, time-boxed credit (“tabs”) to keys they know.
  2. Those claims are assignable (so networks of peers can net obligations).
  3. Only the residual gets settled on Bitcoin (Lightning or on-chain) on a schedule.
  4. Anyone can compute a path across their web of trust to complete a payment without a bank, bridge, or sequencer.
  5. The exit is always there: you can settle and walk away.


Trust is not eliminated, it’s metered.


Mutual credit, in plain language

Think invoices and bar tabs, but cryptographic and routable:

  1. Issue: Alice buys from Bob; Bob issues Alice a signed receipt (Alice owes Bob).
  2. Assign: Bob owes Carol; Bob assigns part of Alice’s IOU to Carol. Now Alice effectively owes Carol.
  3. Net: A chain of assignments cancels many obligations without touching L1.
  4. Settle: Parties periodically pay down deltas over Lightning/on-chain. Anchors (Merkle roots) timestamp the outstanding graph for audit.


Each trust line has caps (how much), windows (how long), and optional witnesses (co-signers for accountability). That’s it. No global state, no consensus beyond Bitcoin.

Result: Most commerce lives in credit & netting; Bitcoin is the settlement court of last resort.


Why this scales and stays sovereign:

  1. Economic density: Netting collapses thousands of interactions into a handful of settlements.
  2. Locality: Credit is local to relationships; risk doesn’t blow out chain-wide.
  3. Modularity: Any community can run routers/witnesses; no single chokepoint.
  4. Ossification-friendly: The base layer stays simple; the fabric evolves at the edges.
  5. Credible exit: Settlement windows are explicit; receipts reference settlement proofs. If trust breaks, you settle and disconnect.


You are not trading “no trust” for “blind trust.” You are trading “global, permanent replication” for small, explicit promises with a bounded blast radius.


A negative example: the “Bitcoin treasury” trend

Newcomers are told to “Bitcoin like a pro” by buying ETF shares, parking BTC with an institution, or adopting corporate treasury “best practices.” It’s sold as sophistication. In practice, it’s a return to legacy finance trust, with the same gatekeepers, legal seizure paths, and socialized failures.


That “scales” adoption statistics, not Bitcoin’s promise. It on-boards people into someone else’s database and calls it victory. If that’s our future, we didn’t fix anything, we re-skinned it.

Mutual credit is the opposite instinct: keep the exit, push coordination to the edges, and publish receipts.


Objections, answered


“Isn’t this just trusting people?”

  1. Yes, in small, timed slices, with receipts and settlement. Trust is a resource; we meter it.


“Won’t defaults happen?”

  1. Inevitably. That’s why caps, windows, witnesses, and reputation exist. Defaults stay local; they don’t nuke a chain or a custodian.


“Is this legal trouble?”

  1. It’s standard commercial credit and assignment. You can add optional arbitration templates where needed. No custody, no pooled deposits.


“Why not a fast sidechain instead?”

  1. You can. But then you trust signers/bridge operators for everything, always. With mutual credit, you trust peers for some amounts for some time, and you keep Bitcoin as the court.


The minimal blueprint (what to actually build)

  1. Receipts: signed claims with issuer, beneficiary, amount/unit, due_by, cap_ref, prev_hash (for assignment), and optional witnesses.
  2. Assignments: change of beneficiary + beneficiary signature; optional witness co-sign.
  3. Anchors: periodic Merkle roots of outstanding receipts posted to Bitcoin (or referenced via a widely witnessed log).
  4. Trust lines: per-peer caps and windows.
  5. Routers: propose assignment paths across local webs; earn tiny fees when paths complete.
  6. Settlement links: attach Lightning/on-chain proofs to receipts as they’re paid down.
  7. UX: “Trust Alice up to 100k sats for 7 days.” “You owe 183k, you’re owed 177k, net now?” “Settle to within 1k sats?” Two taps. Done.


The mental model to take home

  1. Bitcoin scales credibility, not TPS.
  2. Complexity imports trust; own it or it owns you.
  3. Scale = netting + bounded credit + periodic settlement.
  4. Tabs, not chains. Exit, not edicts.


If we build this fabric of plain receipts, assignable claims, small caps, short windows, and an easy path to settle on Bitcoin, we get the scale everyone keeps promising without the centralization they keep delivering.


That’s a world where billions transact every day while the base chain remains sovereign. Not by pretending trust disappeared, but by finally engineering it.


Yes, this whole article is to let you know what we are working on at Synonym, and how to think about it. Instead of being distracted by Bitcoin policy drama, soft-fork narratives, and R&D for complex layers, we are looking deeply, and honestly, at scaling for free markets.


R&D for this work has already begun. If you are interested, agree with this article, and can help, contact me.
